overview.title: How ARC-AGI works, and the ARC Prize
overview.main_topic: The format of ARC-AGI tasks (Figure 19.9), what sets it apart from IQ tests (only unseen tasks, controlled priors through Core Knowledge), and the founding of the ARC Prize Foundation
overview.central_idea: ARC-AGI is an IQ-test-like benchmark of grid puzzles, each defined by a few input-output examples, that measures generalization by testing only on never-seen tasks and controls prior knowledge by assuming only Core Knowledge priors. The ARC Prize competition (2024 onward) adds financial incentives to solve it.
overview.importance: This makes the definition of intelligence from p.604 concrete. Understanding the format explains why ARC-AGI resisted LLM scaling (p.606) and why test-time adaptation helped.
learning_objectives: Describe the structure of an ARC-AGI task and how it is scored
Explain the two features that distinguish ARC-AGI from IQ tests
Explain what Core Knowledge priors are and why controlling priors matters
Describe the purpose of the ARC Prize
prerequisites: Intelligence as an efficiency ratio and the need to fix priors and experience (p.604)

summary:
ARC-AGI is meant to be approachable by both machines and humans and looks like human IQ tests such as **Raven's progressive matrices**. At test time you see a series of **tasks**. Each is explained by three or four **examples**, pairs of an input grid and its output grid (Figure 19.9). You then get a new input grid and have **three tries** to produce the correct output grid.

**Figure 19.9** shows a task: three demonstration pairs (input -> output) and a test input followed by a question mark. In each input, a short light-blue diagonal sits on a black grid with a red wall along one edge; in each output, the diagonal continues as a green line that appears to reflect off the red wall. You must infer the rule from the examples and apply it to the new input.

Two things are unique compared with IQ tests:
1. **Only unseen tasks.** ARC measures generalization by testing only on tasks you've never seen, so it's *a game you can't practice for*, at least in theory. Each task has its own logic that must be understood on the fly; memorizing strategies from past tasks doesn't help.
2. **Controlled prior knowledge.** You never face a problem from scratch. ARC-AGI assumes all test takers start from the same knowledge priors, **Core Knowledge priors**, which represent the knowledge systems humans are born with. Unlike IQ tests, ARC never involves acquired knowledge such as English sentences.

**19.3.5 ARC Prize.** In 2024, to accelerate progress toward AI capable of the fluid abstraction and reasoning ARC-AGI measures, the author and Mike Knoop founded the nonprofit **ARC Prize Foundation**. It runs a yearly competition with a large prize pool (over $1 million in 2024) to incentivize researchers to build AI that can solve ARC-AGI and so display genuine fluid intelligence.

paragraphs.what_it_says: (Completing p.604's sentence: ARC-AGI captures this definition of intelligence.) ARC-AGI is approachable by machines and humans and resembles IQ tests such as Raven's progressive matrices. At test time you see a series of tasks, each explained by three or four examples of an input grid and its output grid (Figure 19.9). You're given a new input grid and three tries to produce the correct output grid before moving on.
paragraphs.what_it_means: Each task is a tiny few-shot learning problem: infer a transformation from a handful of demonstrations, then apply it. The few examples are the experience term of p.604's ratio, and keeping it small means only a system that generalizes efficiently can succeed. The output must be exact (every cell, and the grid size), so partial credit isn't possible.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: This format makes the benchmark usable by both humans and machines, so their performance can be compared, and puts few-shot generalization at the center.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Beyond the book: ARC grids are up to 30x30 cells, with each cell taking one of 10 colors. The original ARC had a public training set and evaluation sets; ARC Prize scoring later used two attempts per test input rather than three.

terminology.meaning: A classic nonverbal IQ test where you pick the pattern that completes a matrix of abstract figures.
A set of demonstration input-output grid pairs plus one or more test inputs, all governed by a single hidden rule.

paragraphs.excerpt: Figure 19.9 An ARC-AGI task: the nature of the task is demonstrated by a couple
paragraphs.what_it_says: Caption: an ARC-AGI task is demonstrated by a couple of input-output pair examples; given a new input, you must construct the corresponding output. The figure shows three pairs and a test input with a '?'.
paragraphs.what_it_means: From the image (our reading): each input has a red wall along one edge and a short light-blue diagonal segment. In the outputs, the diagonal is extended as a green line toward the wall and reflected away from it, like a ball bouncing. The wall is on the right, on the left, then at the bottom in the three pairs, and the test input has a wide red wall on the right. Solving it needs concepts like objects, direction, continuation and reflection, none of which need language or cultural knowledge.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It shows what 'understanding a task on the fly' means: the rule isn't stated anywhere and has to be inferred from very few examples, then applied to a configuration not seen in the examples.

paragraphs.excerpt: Compared to IQ tests, two things are unique about ARC-AGI. First, ARC seeks to
paragraphs.what_it_says: Two things are unique compared with IQ tests. First, ARC measures generalization by testing only on tasks you've never seen. It's a game you can't practice for, at least in theory: each test task has its own logic to understand on the fly, and memorizing strategies from past tasks doesn't help.
paragraphs.what_it_means: On a typical IQ test, practicing similar items does raise scores, because the item types repeat. ARC tries to make each task novel so that practice doesn't transfer through memorization, only through general abilities. 'At least in theory' admits that it's hard to guarantee: tasks may share abstractions, and with enough similar tasks a system could learn their common patterns.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: This is the 'creators could not have anticipated' condition from p.604 put into practice, and the reason ARC-AGI resisted memorization-based scaling (p.606).
paragraphs.technical_idea: Beyond the book: the ARC Prize keeps its evaluation tasks private so they can't leak into training data, which is the practical way of enforcing 'never seen before.'
connections: p.604: test only on tasks the system wasn't trained to handle
p.606: most benchmarks can be hacked via memorization, ARC-AGI is designed to resist it

paragraphs.excerpt: In addition, ARC-AGI tries to control for the prior knowledge that you bring to
paragraphs.what_it_says: Second, ARC-AGI controls for prior knowledge. Nobody approaches a problem entirely from scratch. ARC-AGI assumes all test takers start from Core Knowledge priors, the knowledge systems humans are born with. Unlike IQ tests, ARC-AGI tasks never involve acquired knowledge, such as English sentences.
paragraphs.what_it_means: Since priors count as information in the efficiency ratio (p.604), a fair test has to keep them equal between test takers. Limiting tasks to innate-like knowledge means a human and an AI start from roughly the same footing, and success can't come from knowing a language, facts or cultural conventions.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It makes human-AI comparison meaningful and keeps the large stores of acquired knowledge in LLMs from helping much, which is part of why LLMs scored low on ARC (p.606).
paragraphs.technical_idea: Beyond the book: in 'On the Measure of Intelligence,' the Core Knowledge priors (from developmental psychology, e.g. Spelke) include objectness and basic physics, agentness and goal-directedness, elementary numbers and counting, and basic geometry and topology.

terminology.meaning: The knowledge systems humans are born with, assumed to be the only prior knowledge needed for ARC-AGI.
Knowledge learned through experience or culture, such as language, which ARC-AGI excludes.

connections: p.604: the information side of the efficiency ratio includes innate prior knowledge

paragraphs.excerpt: In 2024, to accelerate progress toward AI systems capable of the kind of fluid
paragraphs.what_it_says: In 2024, the author and Mike Knoop founded the nonprofit ARC Prize Foundation to accelerate progress toward AI capable of the fluid abstraction and reasoning ARC-AGI measures. It runs a yearly competition with a large prize pool (over $1 million in 2024) to incentivize researchers to build AI that solves ARC-AGI and so displays genuine fluid intelligence.
paragraphs.what_it_means: Having set the right target (p.604), the next step is to get researchers to aim at it. A prize is a way to apply the shortcut rule productively: if the metric itself requires generalization, then optimizing it should lead toward intelligence rather than away from it.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: The 2024 competition is what produced the test-time adaptation results discussed on p.606.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Beyond the book: Mike Knoop is a co-founder of Zapier. The 2024 competition ran on Kaggle with a hidden test set and compute limits, which matters given the book's emphasis on efficiency.

terminology.meaning: The ability to reason about and solve novel problems, independent of acquired knowledge.
Nonprofit founded in 2024 by Chollet and Mike Knoop that runs the ARC Prize competition.

concepts.name: ARC-AGI
concepts.definition: A benchmark of grid-transformation tasks, each specified by a few input-output examples, designed to measure generalization on unseen tasks with controlled priors.
concepts.intuition: An IQ test you can't study for and that doesn't use words.
concepts.technical: Each task has three or four demonstration pairs and a test input; the solver gets three tries (per the book) to output the exact grid.
concepts.significance: The book's concrete instrument for measuring intelligence as defined on p.604.
concepts.example: Figure 19.9: extend a diagonal and bounce it off a wall.
concepts.misconception: That ARC is hard for humans. The book says a reader would easily score above 95% on the 2019 version (p.606).

concepts.name: Core Knowledge priors
concepts.definition: The knowledge systems humans are born with, assumed to be the only prior knowledge needed for ARC-AGI.
concepts.intuition: What a young child knows without being taught: objects persist, things can be counted, shapes have sides.
concepts.technical: Fixing priors to this set holds the 'prior knowledge' part of the efficiency ratio constant across humans and machines.
concepts.significance: Makes human-machine comparisons fair and keeps acquired knowledge such as language out of the test.
concepts.example: Recognizing that a cluster of same-colored cells is a single object.
concepts.misconception: That ARC requires no prior knowledge at all; it assumes Core Knowledge and nothing more.

concepts.name: Fluid intelligence
concepts.definition: The ability to solve novel problems by reasoning on the fly, as opposed to applying acquired knowledge or memorized strategies.
concepts.intuition: Figuring out a new puzzle rather than remembering the answer.
concepts.technical: What ARC-AGI aims to measure, by requiring unseen task logic to be understood from a few examples.
concepts.significance: The book's target capability for AI, and what the ARC Prize incentivizes.
concepts.example: Inferring the 'bounce off the wall' rule in Figure 19.9.
concepts.misconception: That broad knowledge implies fluid intelligence; an LLM can have vast knowledge and little fluid intelligence.

concepts.name: ARC Prize
concepts.definition: A yearly competition, run by the nonprofit ARC Prize Foundation (Chollet and Mike Knoop, 2024), with a prize pool over $1 million in 2024 for progress on ARC-AGI.
concepts.intuition: A bounty for building fluid intelligence.
concepts.technical: Aligns researchers' incentives with a metric of generalization rather than task skill.
concepts.significance: Its 2024 results catalyzed the shift to test-time adaptation (p.606).
concepts.example: Top 2024 entries all used test-time adaptation.
concepts.misconception: That it rewards any high score regardless of method; the book's emphasis is on genuine fluid intelligence, and efficiency matters (p.607).

deeper.title: Solving Figure 19.9 step by step
deeper.body:
Our reading of the figure, not stated in the book:
1. **Find the objects** in each input: a red wall along one edge, and a short light-blue diagonal segment.
2. **Compare inputs and outputs**: the light-blue cells stay; new green cells appear that continue the diagonal in the same direction.
3. **Find what happens at the wall**: the green line turns when it meets the red wall and continues diagonally away from it, like a reflection.
4. **Check against all pairs**: the wall is on the right, the left and the bottom in the three examples, and the rule holds each time.
5. **Apply to the test input**: continue its diagonal toward the red wall on the right and reflect it.

Every step uses Core Knowledge (objects, direction, contact), not language or facts.

deeper.title: Why ARC is a few-shot program-induction problem
deeper.body: Beyond the book: each ARC task can be seen as an unknown program f mapping grids to grids. The demonstrations are (input, f(input)) pairs, and the solver must find a program consistent with them and apply it to the test input. With three or four examples, many programs fit; the solver needs strong priors about which programs are 'natural' (Core Knowledge). This framing is why program synthesis and search methods (p.606, p.613) are natural candidates, and why pure interpolation from training data struggles.

deeper.title: A driving test in a city you've never visited
deeper.body: Testing a driver on the same route every time measures memory of the route. Testing them in a new city, with only the rules of driving assumed, measures driving ability. ARC is the new city; Core Knowledge is the rules of driving everyone is assumed to know.

misconceptions.claim: ARC-AGI is just another IQ test.
misconceptions.correction: It resembles IQ tests but differs in two ways: it only tests on tasks never seen before, and it controls prior knowledge by excluding acquired knowledge like language.

misconceptions.claim: You can get good at ARC by memorizing many past tasks.
misconceptions.correction: Each test task has its own logic, so it's 'a game you can't practice for,' at least in theory.

misconceptions.claim: ARC assumes no prior knowledge at all.
misconceptions.correction: It assumes Core Knowledge priors, the knowledge systems humans are born with.

takeaways: An ARC-AGI task gives three or four input-output grid examples, then a new input with three tries to produce the output.
ARC tests only on never-seen tasks, so it can't be practiced for by memorization.
It controls priors: only Core Knowledge, never acquired knowledge like language.
The ARC Prize Foundation (2024, Chollet and Mike Knoop) runs a yearly competition with over $1 million in prizes in 2024.

questions.question: Describe the structure of an ARC-AGI task and how you're scored on it.
questions.answer: Three or four demonstration examples (input grid -> output grid) explain the task; then you get a new input grid and have three tries to produce the exact output grid.
questions.explanation: From the first paragraph of the page and Figure 19.9.

questions.question: Which of these is NOT one of the two features the book says make ARC-AGI unique compared to IQ tests?
options: It only tests on tasks you've never seen before
It controls for prior knowledge using Core Knowledge priors
It excludes acquired knowledge like English sentences
It is designed to be difficult for humans
questions.answer: It is designed to be difficult for humans
questions.explanation: The two features are testing only on unseen tasks and controlling for prior knowledge (of which excluding acquired knowledge is part). ARC is meant to be approachable by humans, who score very high (p.606).

questions.question: Why does ARC-AGI exclude acquired knowledge such as English sentences?
questions.answer: Because prior knowledge counts as information in the efficiency ratio of intelligence. To compare test takers fairly, they must start from the same priors, here the innate Core Knowledge. Acquired knowledge would let a system score by what it already knows rather than by generalizing.
questions.explanation: Links p.605's design choice to p.604's definition.

questions.question: Why does the book say ARC-AGI is a game you can't practice for 'at least in theory'?
questions.answer: Because each test task has its own unique logic to understand on the fly, so memorized strategies shouldn't transfer. 'In theory' acknowledges that tasks may still share abstractions or patterns, so perfect novelty can't be guaranteed.
questions.explanation: The book's qualification suggests novelty is a design goal, not an absolute property.

questions.question: What was the purpose of founding the ARC Prize Foundation in 2024?
options: To sell ARC-AGI as a commercial IQ test
To accelerate progress toward AI capable of fluid abstraction and reasoning by incentivizing researchers
To replace ImageNet as the main computer-vision benchmark
To certify AI systems as AGI
questions.answer: To accelerate progress toward AI capable of fluid abstraction and reasoning by incentivizing researchers
questions.explanation: The page says so directly. The foundation is a nonprofit (not commercial), ARC isn't a vision benchmark in the ImageNet sense, and nothing on the page mentions certification.

questions.question: Look at Figure 19.9 and try to produce the output for the test input before reading any explanation. What concepts did you use?
questions.answer: Open-ended; typical concepts are objects, direction, continuing a line, and reflecting off a wall.
questions.explanation: Noticing that you used only innate-like concepts shows what Core Knowledge priors mean.
